# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up is careful and settles several open questions, mostly in the direction the evidence pointed. The rebuttals of both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are largely fair, and the arithmetic checks out. **The issues to raise are:**
- The Summary compares two different hours measures, which overstates the decline.
- Control offices changed their own meeting practices partway through. This affects how the decline should be read.
- The mediation result is less independent and less precise than "confirms" implies.
- The Halden follow-up has selection problems that aren't fully acknowledged.

## Arithmetic check

These reproduce correctly:
- Output per hour on timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%**.
- Output per hour on system logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%**.
- Halden continuers: 0.968 / 0.866 = **+11.8%**, with hours 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%.
- Mediation shares sum to 100% (47 + 18 + 35).
- Meetings difference-in-differences: −3.5 h minus −0.2 h = **−3.3 h**. This matches the month-six gap in the nine-month report.

## Main problems

**1. The Summary compares two different hours measures.**
- The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% … to 8.5%". That compares nine-month *timesheet* hours with 24-month *log* hours.
- On the same measure (timesheets), the decline is 12.5% → 9.8%. That is a fall of about a fifth, not a third.
- Section 5's "about a quarter" matches neither figure.
- The body text handles this correctly. The Summary should match it: 12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets, with 8.5% on the stricter log measure.

**2. Changes in two control offices may account for part of the "decay".**
In month 15, two control offices cancelled standing meetings and raised their output per hour by about 4.1%. That is a change in the comparison group, quite possibly prompted by the trial itself. This has three consequences:
- It lowers the 24-month difference-in-differences estimate. A rough calculation: 2 of 7 offices × 4.1% ≈ 1.2% on the control average. That could be close to half of the 12.5% → 9.8% decline.
- The decline therefore isn't purely treated offices fading. Part of it may be control offices improving.
- The 8.5% may be slightly conservative as an estimate of the effect of reduced hours.

The authors should report:
- the treated-only trend
- a sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices

One further check: if those two offices are at 5.0 h and the control mean is 7.0 h, the other five control offices must average about 7.8 h. That is *up* from a 7.2 h baseline. The authors should confirm this.

**3. The mediation result is a pre-specified test, not an independent replication.**
- Registering at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes, is good practice.
- But the test uses the *same seven treated offices* that generated the hypothesis. The re-analysis's core concern was replication on new units, and this doesn't provide it.
- "Larger sample of office-months" overstates precision. Treatment and mostly the mediator vary at office level, so the effective sample is 14 clusters. A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The authors should state how they accounted for clustering and repeated measures.
- "Confirms" is too strong. "Supports, in a pre-specified test on the same offices" would be accurate.

**4. A simple accounting check gives a much larger meetings share than 47%.**
- Rough working: log hours fell about 4.2 h/week from about 37.9 h, and meetings fell 3.3 h.
- That puts the fall in non-meeting hours at about 3%. Output per FTE fell 3.4%.
- So if meetings produced no case output, the meeting cut alone would account for **essentially all** of the per-hour gain.
- The model's 47% may still be right. Meetings may have had some productive value, or measurement error in the mediator may shrink the estimated share.
- But the gap between roughly 100% and 47% is large and should be reconciled. It matters for the policy question raised in the unplanned observation: how much of the gain could be had by cutting meetings without cutting hours?

**5. The Halden follow-up's selection and framing need tightening.**
- **Non-response.** Of the 23 organisations contacted, 9 didn't respond. Non-responders are likely to include more of the organisations that reverted, so 3 of 14 understates the reversion rate.
- **The "coverage" label is stretched.** The Summary says all reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But the marketing agency gave client deadlines as its reason, and marketing was coded *discretionary* in the meta-analysis. Widening the category after the fact to cover all three reverters weakens the coverage-bound story rather than confirming it.
- **Baseline hours.** The continuers' baseline of 40.3 h equals the re-analysis's 27-organisation baseline exactly. Is this these 11 organisations' own baseline?
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** These are survivors with no control group, so "likely optimistic" is more accurate. Secular productivity trends and other uncontrolled factors could push the figure in either direction.
- **The misreported attrition is still unaddressed.** Okafor is a Halden author and co-authors this report. It would be the natural place to respond to the re-analysis's finding that withdrawals were misdescribed, and it doesn't.

**6. The counter-arm cost figure needs explaining.**
- Restoring output after a −11.4% per-FTE drop needs about 1 / 0.886 ≈ 12.9% more staff. The county's 12% is in line with that.
- At full pay, that should raise labour cost per contact by about 12%, not 9%.
- 9% is plausible only if non-staff costs are about a quarter of total cost. The paper should say so.

## Smaller points

- **Baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Where do the baseline figures (7.4 h and 7.2 h) come from? If calendars were retrieved retrospectively, the report should say so. These figures also resolve the concern I raised earlier: baseline meeting time was balanced between arms.
- **Two time points can't show a trend.** Nine and 24 months can't distinguish a gain that plateaued from one still declining. Monthly timesheet-based estimates should be reported. "Not consistent with zero by month ten" is correct, but it doesn't rule out continued fading after month 24.
- **Sick days.** The −27% still carries the mechanical problem: fewer scheduled days mean fewer possible sick days.
- **Limitations section.** It omits the control-office contamination, clustering in the mediation analysis, non-response in the Halden follow-up, and the change of hours measure between time points.

## How the earlier claims stand now

**The re-analysis.**
- The rebuttal is fair. The Varden 24-month estimate meets the standards the re-analysis itself set: randomised, record-based output, log-measured hours, two years of follow-up. It still finds +8.5%.
- The re-analysis was right that headline figures were inflated, and partly right about fading.
- It was wrong that nothing remains, and wrong to dismiss the meetings mechanism, although the evidence for meetings is still weaker than "confirms" suggests.

**The meta-analysis.**
- The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.
- That confirms the duration analysis couldn't speak to decay, which was the main problem I flagged.
- The one controlled long follow-up shows modest decline. Some of that decline may be the control offices improving rather than treated offices fading.

**Updated synthesis across all five documents:**

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8.5–10% at 24 months (randomised). Down from about 12.5% at 9 months, partly because control offices improved |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Roughly flat to slightly negative (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2) |
| Coverage-bound work | Per-worker output falls about 9–11% and service worsens. Varden ended the arm; restoring service costs about 9–12% per contact |
| Durability | Gain persists to 24 months but has declined somewhat. Trend beyond 24 months unknown |
| Mechanism | Reduced meeting time is the leading candidate, but replication on new units is needed. Fatigue plays a smaller role. About a third is unexplained |
| Gain without cutting hours? | Open. The two-office meeting audit suggests partly yes, but no trial arm has tested it |

The obvious next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, reorganisation (including a meeting audit) without reduced hours, and control. It is the only design that can tell whether the hours cut is what drives the gain or what makes the reorganisation happen.

If useful, I can draft a referee report on this follow-up, or a consolidated evidence brief covering all five documents.
